q-78294.name: Question 1
q-78294.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}60 \\ 144\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
q-78294.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot [\begin{aligned}60 \\ 144\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{12}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{12}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{12}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-159761.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 12\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 8\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
q-159761.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{2}{3}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{2}{3}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-78295.name: Question 3
q-78295.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-54 \\ 81\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 9\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
q-78295.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-54 \\ 81\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{9}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{9}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-78255.name: Question 4
q-78255.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-35 \\ -25\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -5\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
q-78255.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-35 \\ -25\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{5}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{5}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

A linear transformation T represents a dilation. Given that v=[−35−25] and T(v)=[−7−5], what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[151115]
b
[015150]
c
[150015]
d
[155515]
e
[5005]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can write T(v) as follows:

T(v)=[−7−5]=15⋅[−35−25]=15v

So we have T(v)=15v, and so the linear transformation T is a dilation with scale factor k=15.

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor k is given by [k00k].

Therefore, the standard matrix of T is T=[150015].

q-78253.name: Question 5
q-78253.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-60 \\ -9\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ -3\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
q-78253.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-60 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{3}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{3}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

A linear transformation T represents a dilation. Given that v=[−60−9] and T(v)=[−20−3], what is the standard matrix of T?

[130013]

[131113]
d

T(v)=[−20−3]=13⋅[−60−9]=13v

So we have T(v)=13v, and so the linear transformation T is a dilation with scale factor k=13.

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor k is given by [k00k].

Therefore, the standard matrix of T is T=[130013].

q-8060.name: Question 8
q-8060.problem: What linear transformation $T$ is represented by the matrix $T=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
q-8060.worked_solution:
Consider the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ of the Euclidean plane ${R}^{2}$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242551/assets/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

Now, we compute the images of $\{i,j\}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain the following image:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242551/assets/4a83673a409fd2e5d33b0b5f743f57af08cfb27c38e312a636179102c2172b04.png)

Therefore, the matrix represents a reflection in the line $y=-x.$

The correct answer is $T=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$ Indeed, consider the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ of the Euclidean plane ${R}^{2}$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242551/assets/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

Now, we can find the images of $\{i,j\}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i\end{aligned}
$$
